title: Section 133 — Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation

content.overview: BNS s. 133 — Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation. BNS restatement of IPC 355. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 355. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 133 is the rule on “Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation”. The section provides that whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 133 exists so that “Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

learningObjectives: Master the aggravated offence of assaulting or using criminal force with intent to dishonour under BNS s. 133.
Analyze the specific mens rea: intending thereby to dishonour that person.
Examine the two-year imprisonment tier, fine, or both.
Understand the application to public humiliation, blackening faces, or garlanding with shoes.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 133 penalizes whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protects personal dignity and reputation by imposing aggravated penalties when physical force or assault is weaponized specifically to publicly humiliate and dishonour a victim.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 133 (corresponding to IPC s. 355).
Actus reus: Assaulting (s. 130) or using criminal force (s. 129).
Specific mens rea: Intending thereby to dishonour that person.
Condition: Committed otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation.
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description extending up to two years, or fine, or both.
essentialIngredients: The accused assaulted or used criminal force against the victim.
The act was done with the specific intention of dishonouring the victim.
The act was committed otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 133 carries forward Section 355 of the IPC. While simple assault under Section 131 is punished with up to three months, Section 133 elevates the punishment to two years imprisonment when the assault or force is motivated by an intent to dishonour, humiliate, or disgrace the victim. The essence of the offence is the attack on human dignity. Common manifestations include parading someone with a blackened face, garlanding a person with old shoes, spitting in someone's face in public, or throwing ink or cow dung. The prosecution must establish that the dominant intent was social or personal humiliation rather than ordinary anger or physical injury.
examples: Teaching example (Garlanding with footwear): An accused leads a crowd into a municipal office, catches a government official, and forcibly places a garland made of old shoes around his neck while recording a video to circulate on social media. The accused is liable under s. 133 (up to two years).
Teaching example (Blackening face): Assailants forcibly smear black shoe polish over a victim's face in a crowded village square to shame him regarding a disputed loan. This satisfies s. 133.
distinctions: Section 133 vs Section 131: Section 131 applies to simple unprovoked assault (up to 3 months); Section 133 applies when the specific intent is to dishonour (up to 2 years).
Section 133 vs Defamation (s. 356): Defamation involves spoken or written words injuring reputation; Section 133 involves physical assault or criminal force intended to dishonour.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who publicly threw a glass of ink into a college professor's face during an assembly to humiliate him committed an offence under s. 133.
Rule: Using criminal force with intent to dishonour a person constitutes an offence under BNS s. 133.
Application: Throwing ink is criminal force, executed publicly with deliberate intent to dishonour the professor.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty under BNS s. 133 and faces up to two years imprisonment.
